item.research_question: Does extreme plastic deformation induce solid-state amorphization in the equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy, and what are the mechanisms and mechanical implications of this transformation?
item.processing_route: Vacuum induction melting and spray forming followed by swaging to a cold work strain of ~80% (nominal strain 0.8); subsequent testing via quasi-static uniaxial compression (strain rate 10⁻³ s⁻¹), dynamic uniaxial compression (strain rate 1.7 × 10³ s⁻¹), and dynamic shear using forced hat-shaped geometry (shear strain rate 6 × 10⁵ s⁻¹, local strain >1.5)
item.test_conditions: Quasi-static compression at room temperature; dynamic compression and shear at initial temperature of 77 K; strain rates ranging from 10⁻³ s⁻¹ to 6 × 10⁵ s⁻¹; strains up to 1.5
key_findings: Amorphous islands of roughly 10 nm size and amorphous bands were observed in highly deformed regions, confirmed by high-resolution TEM and Fourier-transformed diffractographs showing diffuse scattering.
The alloy exhibited high strength between 1 and 2 GPa across all strain rates, with quasi-static work hardening continuing up to a strain of 0.8 despite pre-deformation.
In dynamic shear experiments, the equivalent strain reached 1.5, significantly higher than in quasi-static tests, leading to adiabatic shear localization.
The volume fraction of amorphous material scales with the intersections of deformation bands containing stacking faults, twins, and hcp ε-martensite.
The absorbed deviatoric strain energy (area under shear stress-strain curves) for predeformed materials was approximately 3200 MPa, roughly twice that of the fully annealed alloy (~1600 MPa).
No apparent chemical segregation was found in the vicinity of amorphous materials, suggesting the amorphization is deformation-induced rather than a preparation artifact.
The critical dislocation density for the fcc→hcp transformation was predicted to be ρ ~ 8 × 10¹⁵ m⁻² based on a stacking-fault energy of ~20 mJ m⁻².
item.mechanism: The authors propose that coordinated propagation of stacking faults and twins along {111} planes generates high-deformation regions that reorganize into hexagonal packets; when the defect density reaches a critical level, the free energy of the heavily deformed fcc/hcp structures becomes comparable to that of the amorphous phase, triggering a solid-state transformation to amorphous material at the intersections of these deformation bands.
item.limitations: The authors state that determining the precise parameters for the sigmoidal relationship between amorphous volume fraction and plastic strain requires significant and systematic efforts using displacement-controlled experiments, which is nontrivial for dynamic testing.
item.future_work: The authors propose tailoring the composition to further lower the stacking-fault energy and optimizing thermal-mechanical treatment to introduce higher defect densities to maximize beneficial effects for creating new alloys designed for extreme loading environments.
quotes: When the defect density in these regions reaches a critical level, they generate islands of amorphous material.
We provide evidence here that under very high strain-rate loading, the TRIP effect can be observed in the Cantor alloy.
